This narrative review explores how estrogen influences lysyl oxidase function, particularly in the context of collagen crosslinking and connective tissue health. Special emphasis is placed on biological female anterior cruciate ligament injury risk, a highly relevant example of clinical estrogen-associated extracellular matrix vulnerability. By integrating epidemiologic evidence with emerging molecular and mechanistic data, clinicians are provided with a contemporary biologically informed perspective on sex-specific anterior cruciate ligament injury risk. Future research and prevention strategies are discussed.

records.title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
records.abstract: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol. Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength. There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status. MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants. (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals. II.

records.title: Exposure-adjusted injury incidence and the impact of surveillance definitions in handball: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
records.abstract: Handball carries a substantial injury burden, though reported incidence varies. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified exposure-adjusted injury incidence in handball by synthesizing prospective cohort studies. Sixteen studies (11,049 players) were included. The pooled overall injury incidence was 5.05 per 1,000 hours; however, substantial heterogeneity was observed and prediction intervals were wide. Match incidence was significantly higher than training incidence, and contact injuries exceeded non-contact injuries. Notably, the difference between non-time-loss and time-loss injuries was not statistically significant (p = 0.058). Back players had significantly higher match injury rates than goalkeepers, and elite players exceeded amateurs. The knee and ankle were the most frequently injured anatomical locations, predominantly sustaining contusions and sprains. These findings emphasize the need for standardized surveillance and targeted prevention for match-related contact injuries, while highlighting that pooled rates require cautious interpretation due to extreme between-study variability.

records.title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
records.abstract: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects. This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

records.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of AI-Generated Personalized Sleep Feedback in High School Female Soccer Players: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract: Adequate sleep supports mood regulation and injury prevention in high school female athletes; however, insufficient sleep is common in this population. Wearable devices enable continuous assessment of objective sleep metrics, but personalized feedback based on daily sleep data remains underexplored. This study evaluated the technical and operational feasibility of a multicomponent AI-supported mobile health (mHealth) intervention that delivered personalized sleep feedback to high school female soccer players. Sleep efficiency was the primary preliminary efficacy outcome; other sleep-related measures were secondary or exploratory outcomes, and mood state and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes. We conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial among 25 high school female soccer players from a single team. The study briefing and system setup began on August 18, 2025, and the trial was retrospectively registered with the University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN) Clinical Trials Registry on April 7, 2026 (UMIN000061189). Weeks 1 to 4 constituted the baseline period. After the week 5 baseline questionnaires, participants were stratified by median baseline total sleep time (TST) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score and randomly allocated 1:1 to the intervention (n=12) or control (n=13) group. During weeks 6 to 9, the intervention group received GPT-4o-generated personalized feedback via LINE on days with valid prior-night Fitbit data, whereas the control group received daily nonpersonalized sleep information. Technical and operational feasibility outcomes included message delivery success, valid Fitbit wear nights, questionnaire completion, technical problems, adverse events, and privacy breaches. Secondary outcomes included TST, wake after sleep onset (WASO), subjective sleep quality, sleep difficulty, and daytime sleepiness. Deep, light, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep durations, mood state, and sports injury severity were exploratory outcomes. All 25 participants completed the trial. Message delivery success and questionnaire completion were 100% in both groups. Median valid Fitbit wear nights were 26 (IQR 24-28) in the intervention group and 22 (IQR 15-26) in the control group. No major technical problems, adverse events, or privacy breaches occurred. Change in sleep efficiency, the primary preliminary efficacy outcome, favored the intervention group (Hodges-Lehmann between-group difference 2%, 95% CI 0.50%-4%; P=.046; r=0.35). Nominal between-group differences were also observed for the Japanese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI-J) total score and sleep difficulty score and, among exploratory outcomes, REM sleep duration and total mood disturbance. No between-group differences were observed in TST, WASO, deep or light sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, or sports injury severity. The multicomponent AI-supported mHealth intervention demonstrated technical and operational feasibility in this single-team setting. Preliminary, hypothesis-generating between-group differences were observed in sleep efficiency and selected subjective sleep and mood outcomes. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of established effectiveness and require confirmation in a sufficiently powered trial. UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000061189; https://tinyurl.com/tw3d7aku.

records.title: Feedforward Pre-Activation of Lateral Ankle Muscles Is Insufficient Against Excessive Ankle Inversion During Perturbation in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability.
records.abstract: This study aimed to compare ankle kinematics and muscle activation between individuals with and without chronic ankle instability (CAI), both prior to and following landing on an inversion trapdoor during walking, with a particular focus on the feedforward pre-activation of lateral ankle muscles and the consequent ankle kinematics post-perturbation. Forty participants were enrolled, including 20 with CAI and 20 age- and sex-matched non-CAI controls. They walked at their own pace on a custom-designed walking platform equipped with a trapdoor programmed to trigger a 24° inversion perturbation, simulating lateral ankle sprain conditions, across three unanticipated trials. Their lower limb muscle electromyography and ankle kinematics were synchronously collected 200 ms pre- and 200 ms post-perturbation. Continuous between-group data were compared by independent sample t-tests. CAI individuals showed higher pre-activation in the peroneus longus (-200.0 to -196.4 ms, mean diff: -11.38%, p = 0.049; -54.6 to -11.0 ms, mean diff: -10.60%, p = 0.011) and the lateral gastrocnemius (-200.0 to -175.4 ms, mean diff: -7.62%, p = 0.029) prior to perturbation, and lower activation in the peroneus longus at 72.1 to 98.0 ms (mean diff: 17.46%, p = 0.029) post-perturbation. They also showed greater ankle inversion in four clusters post-perturbation (0 to 111.0 ms, mean diff: -4.85°, p < 0.001; 117.0 to 128.0 ms, mean diff: -1.83°, p = 0.020; 142.0 to 145.0 ms, mean diff: -1.30°, p = 0.047; 154.0 to 165.0 ms, mean diff: -1.05°, p = 0.019). CAI individuals exhibit higher feedforward pre-activation in lateral ankle muscles, which may be insufficient against excessive ankle inversion after landing on a trapdoor during walking.

records.title: Flexible and stretchable bioelectronics for sports wearable monitoring: Materials, Device Engineering, and Intelligent Wearable Platforms.
records.abstract: Modern sports science is undergoing a paradigm shift from subjective coaching to objective, data-driven precision training. Consequently, wearable electronics for acquiring precise data during sports activities are attracting attention. However, conventional rigid wearables inherently suffer from mechanical mismatches between rigid wearables and the soft, deformable human skin, inducing severe motion artifacts and restricting natural biomechanics during high-intensity athletic activities. To address these limitations from a comprehensive perspective, this review systematically summarizes and analyzes recent advancements in next-generation flexible and stretchable bioelectronics tailored specifically for sports applications. We systematically examine the substrate materials, structural engineering designs, and device-level optimization strategies required to withstand repetitive strain, shear, and sweat-intensive environments. Building upon these conformable bio-interfaces, we discuss three core sensing modalities: electrochemical sensors for real-time analysis of sweat biomarkers, biophysical sensors for continuous electrophysiological and hemodynamic monitoring, and electromechanical sensors for high-fidelity kinematic and impact tracking. Furthermore, we discuss body-derived energy harvesting strategies to power sports wearables and wireless communication systems for continuous athletic monitoring. The importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning is increasing, as these techniques enable the removal of motion artifacts and facilitate objective analysis of athletic data for training and health monitoring applications. By evaluating targeted applications across aerobic and anaerobic exercise, cognitive state assessment, and post-exercise recovery, this review demonstrates how next-generation sports wearables contribute to the shift in sports science from reactive treatment toward proactive, data-driven performance enhancement and injury prevention.

records.title: From Sprain to End-Stage Osteoarthritis: Why Earlier Intervention in Ankle Cartilage Damage Deserves More Attention.
records.abstract: ➢ Ankle cartilage damage ranges from osteochondral lesions of the talus to end-stage osteoarthritis. End-stage ankle osteoarthritis has been associated with a health burden comparable with that of major chronic diseases such as congestive heart failure and kidney disease, while predominantly affecting young and active patients.➢ Ankle osteoarthritis often has a posttraumatic nature, making it possible to study the long-term results of traumatic articular injuries and identify potential targets for early therapeutic interventions.➢ The scientific literature has been predominantly focused on outcomes after surgical treatment of osteochondral lesions of the talus or osteoarthritis. However, evidence on nonoperative treatment has been limited and methodologically weak, with evidence for early interventions (e.g., lifestyle or biologicals) even more scarce.➢ The greatest opportunity to improve long-term outcomes in ankle cartilage damage may be early recognition and early initiation of treatment.

records.title: Global Research Trends in Metatarsal Stress Fractures in Athletes.
records.abstract: Metatarsal Stress Fractures (MSFs) are commonly occurring overuse injuries for athletes and soldiers. This paper investigated publication patterns, top authors, networks, and themes associated with MSFs. Bibliometric analysis of publications on MSFs published during the period from 1970-2026 was carried out using the Web of Science Core Collection. Network and visualization of bibliometric analyses were carried out using VOSviewer. A total of 479 publications were identified. There has been a significant rise in research output following 2011, peaking during 2017-2025 years. Subject categories with highest publication outputs were Orthopedics and Sport Sciences; the most active countries are the United States, England, and Japan; JA Nunley is the most prolific author, whereas Foot & Ankle International is the most popular journal; keywords include Jones' fractures, 5th metatarsal fracture, surgical intervention, and return to play. Increase in publication outputs likely reflects rising sports participation levels and advances in sports medicine. Nevertheless, the majority of research is centered around Jones' fractures, surgery, with minimal interest in preventive strategies, metabolism-related risk factors, and minor metatarsal stress fractures. Future research should focus on prevention methods, metabolism, and scientific approaches to returning to sport activities.

records.title: How resistive ankle exoskeleton training affects walking outcomes in cerebral palsy.
records.abstract: Improving walking ability is a central goal in the clinical management of cerebral palsy (CP). The objective of this study was to assess how gait training with a resistive ankle exoskeleton affects walking performance in individuals with CP. Sixteen ambulatory individuals (GMFCS levels I-III) with CP between the ages of 8 and 21 completed the study. Participants completed a pre-training assessment and then 12 sessions of treadmill-based gait training with the Biomotum Spark ankle exoskeleton providing plantarflexor resistance with plantar-pressure biofeedback. Outcomes were assessed during walking without ankle resistance before, and at follow-up visits within one week and three weeks after training. Ankle-resisted gait training had a positive effect on most mobility-related outcome measures. 6MWT distance increased by 17% (p = 0.02) on the post vs baseline assessment. Self-selected walking speed increased by 16% (p = 0.003) and 23% (p < 0.001) on the within-1-week post and 3-week post assessments, respectively, compared to baseline. Fast walking speed increased by 10% (p = 0.008) and 17% (p = 0.016) on the within-1-week post and 3-week post assessments, respectively, compared to baseline. Gait training with a resistive ankle exoskeleton providing biofeedback elicited clinically significant improvements in walking endurance and speed. These results demonstrate the clinical safety and efficacy of gait training with ankle exoskeleton resistance in CP.

records.title: Ilizarov Circular Fixation for High-Velocity Firearm Injuries Causing High-Energy Tibial Fractures: A Prospective Cohort Study.
records.abstract: High-velocity gunshot tibial fractures present major reconstructive challenges owing to extensive contamination, soft-tissue devitalisation, and segmental bone loss that render early internal fixation hazardous. We aimed to document outcomes of a structured Ilizarov-based protocol for this injury type and describe a reproducible treatment framework for resource-constrained settings. Between January 2019 and December 2023, we prospectively enrolled 20 adult male patients with open tibial fractures from high-velocity firearm injuries at three Cairo trauma centres; all were treated definitively with an Ilizarov circular external fixator, with distraction osteogenesis and fibular autografting were employed selectively for segmental bone loss. The primary outcome was fracture union rate; secondary outcomes included fixation duration, surgical burden, and complications. Mean age was 29.7 ± 8.4 years. Fourteen fractures (70%) were Gustilo-Anderson type IIIA and six (30%) type IIIB; bone defects were present in 50% after debridement. Union was achieved in 19 of 20 patients (95%), and the single non-union resolved after frame revision and supplementary grafting. Mean fixation duration was 12.3 ± 7.28 months. Superficial pin-tract infection (Checketts-Otterburn Grade 1 or 2) occurred in 17 patients (85%) and deep surgical site infection in one (5%); ankle stiffness, axial malalignment, and limb length discrepancy each affected a minority of patients. structured Ilizarov protocol can reliably achieve union in Gustilo type III gunshot tibial fractures with an acceptable complication profile; these findings are descriptive and do not establish superiority over alternative fixation strategies but support the Ilizarov circular frame as a suitable option for high-grade contaminated injuries in resource-limited environments.

records.title: Impact of foot orthoses hindfoot and forefoot wedges on foot and ankle kinematics: A cadaveric study.
records.abstract: Foot orthoses (FOs) are widely prescribed to manage musculoskeletal and inflammatory disorders affecting the lower limbs by modifying foot and ankle biomechanics. While the addition of medial wedges to FOs is believed to enhance control of pronation-related movements, few studies have quantified their isolated kinematic effects under controlled experimental conditions. The use of cadaveric models allows for precise measurement of bone motion without soft tissue artifacts. Therefore, this study aimed to quantify the effects of 3D-printed FOs with and without a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge on foot and ankle kinematics in cadaveric specimens during quasi-dynamic loading. It was hypothesized that a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge would better prevent both forefoot dorsiflexion and ankle eversion in cadaveric specimens. Nine fresh-frozen lower limbs were tested under three randomized conditions: shoe-only (control), standard FOs (SFO), and medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge FOs (MWFO). FOs were 3D printed in PA11 using the multi-jet fusion technology. Specimens were mounted on a mechanical press with simulated muscle tension applied through tendon loading. Kinematic data were collected via a six-camera motion capture system and reflective markers attached to bone-anchored rods. Ankle and forefoot/hindfoot angles and ranges of motion were calculated in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Non-parametric Friedman ANOVAs and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to assess between-condition differences (α < 0.05). Compared to the control condition, MWFOs significantly reduced peak ankle dorsiflexion (1.40° ± 3.76° vs 3.54° ± 2.74°, p < 0.001) and increased ankle inversion (9.12° ± 11.13° vs 7.09° ± 11.73°, p = 0.002). MWFOs also increased forefoot/hindfoot plantarflexion (p = 0.018) and adduction (p = 0.018) relative to the control condition. No significant differences in joint range of motion were observed across conditions. The addition of a hindfoot-forefoot medial wedge to 3D-printed FOs modifies ankle and midfoot kinematics under quasi-dynamic loading, primarily by reducing pronation-related movements such as dorsiflexion and eversion. These findings support the biomechanical rationale for incorporating hindfoot-forefoot medial wedges in FOs design to enhance control of foot and ankle motion.

records.title: In-lab assessment of a ice hockey helmet-integrated sensor fusion framework for torque estimation: A proof-of-concept study.
records.abstract: This study presents a proof-of-concept ice hockey helmet-integrated system for characterizing in-lab rotational loading, consisting of a single Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) and custom soft foam force sensors. A total of 72 controlled pendulum impacts (33 J and 79 J) were delivered to a helmeted Anthropomorphic Test Device (ATD) at side and crown locations. A custom algorithm detected impacts and estimated torque by combining IMU-derived directions with force magnitudes. Results showed successful discrimination between conditions, with crown impacts producing lower torque. Recognizing torque as a relevant metric may improve monitoring and prevention of brain injury in contact sports.

records.title: Injuries to High School Football Players in Long Island, New York: A Five-Year Study.
records.abstract: Background American football has the highest injury rate of any U.S. high school sport, yet most studies examine a single injury type or position. We characterized injury patterns among high school football athletes in Long Island, New York, over five consecutive seasons, focusing on how injury patterns vary by level of play, setting, and position. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, certified athletic trainers and sports medicine physicians documented all in-season injuries among varsity and junior varsity (JV) athletes at 16 high schools from 2019 to 2023. Level of play, setting, mechanism, anatomic location, diagnosis, position, and time to return to play were recorded. Proportions were compared using two-sample Z-tests for independent proportions, with a two-sided p < 0.05 considered significant. Test statistics are reported as Z values alongside exact p-values. Results Among 3,861 athletes (2,093 varsity, 54.2%), 1,476 injuries were recorded. Varsity athletes accounted for a greater share of injuries than JV athletes (n = 1,104, 74.8% vs. n = 372, 25.2%; Z = 26.95, p < 0.001). Most injuries occurred in games despite far more practices (n = 732 of 1,308 injuries with setting recorded, 56.0%; Z = 6.10, p < 0.001). Direct contact was the leading mechanism (n = 796 of 1,344 injuries with the mechanism recorded, 59.2%). The lower extremity was most often injured (n = 672, 45.5%), followed by the upper extremity (n = 431, 29.2%) and head/neck (n = 187, 12.7%). Concussion was the most common specific diagnosis (n = 131, 8.9%). Profiles differed by position: offensive linemen had the highest proportion of concussions, and linebackers had the highest proportion of contact-related injuries. The proportion of athletes with a recorded concussion did not differ between varsity and JV athletes (Z = 0.53, p = 0.594). Conclusions A greater proportion of recorded injuries occurred among varsity athletes, in games, and through direct contact. Injury profiles differed by position, most notably a high proportion of concussions among offensive linemen. Because athlete exposure denominators were unavailable, these findings describe the distribution of recorded injuries rather than exposure-adjusted risk. These multiyear, position-specific data can inform targeted prevention and safety policy in high school football.

records.title: Injury Patterns, In-Hospital Outcomes, and Resource Utilization of Acute Cuboid and Navicular Fractures.
records.abstract: Acute cuboid and navicular fractures can be serious injuries. However, multicenter data on their associated injuries and in-hospital course are limited. To characterize the demographics, injury patterns, in-hospital outcomes, and resource utilization of trauma center patients with acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Retrospective cross-sectional database study. The American College of Surgeons National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2019) was queried for acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Multivariable regression identified factors associated with discharge to post-acute care, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and hospital length of stay in adults. Overall, 3,424 patients with 4,084 fractures were identified (2,327 with cuboid and 1,637 with navicular fractures, including 540 with both). Road-traffic mechanisms accounted for 64.5%, and 25.1% had polytrauma. Metatarsal, calcaneal, and talar fractures were the most common concomitant injuries. Combined fractures were more often ipsilateral than contralateral (457 vs 18 patients). Despite infrequent complications, 50.2% were discharged home without post-acute services (home health, inpatient rehabilitation, or skilled nursing care). In-hospital mortality was 1.1%. After adjustment, polytrauma (OR 3.75, 95% CI 3.04-4.61), bilateral involvement, and ankle, tibia, fibula, or metatarsal fractures were associated with discharge to post-acute care, whereas fracture pattern was not. Cuboid and navicular fractures are predominantly high-energy injuries that rarely occur in isolation. Post-acute care needs, ICU admission, and length of stay were associated with overall injury burden rather than the specific bone fractured.

records.title: Long-Term Injury Patterns and Trends in Elite Professional Football: A Nine-Season Retrospective Analysis of Prospectively Recorded Data.
records.abstract: Long-term injury surveillance in professional football is essential for understanding temporal changes in injury patterns. However, prospective studies spanning multiple consecutive seasons within the same professional club remain scarce. This study aimed to investigate injury epidemiology, temporal trends, and injury characteristics over nine consecutive seasons in an elite Croatian professional football club. This retrospective longitudinal study over nine competitive seasons (2015/16-2023/24) included 167 male players participating in the professional first-team environment from a single professional football club, contributing a total of 382 player-seasons across nine consecutive seasons. A total of 749 time-loss injuries were recorded according to the FIFA Medical Assessment and Research Centre (F-MARC) consensus recommendations. Temporal trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression, while injury characteristics, anatomical distribution, tissue involvement, and injury burden were analysed descriptively. Overall injury incidence averaged 12.66 injuries per 1000 h of exposure (95% CI: 11.77-13.60), with substantially higher incidence during matches (50.13 injuries/1000 h) than training (7.97 injuries/1000 h). Joinpoint regression identified a non-significant annual decline in injury incidence before the COVID-19 season (2019/2020) (APC = -9.66%), followed by a non-significant increase thereafter (APC = 4.88%). At least one injury was recorded in 295 player-seasons, corresponding to 77.2% of all eligible player-seasons. More than 80% of all injuries involved the lower extremities, while muscle injuries accounted for almost half of all recorded injuries. Functional muscle disorders were the most frequent injury type, whereas meniscal and articular cartilage injuries were associated with the highest mean time loss per injury. The predominance of lower-limb muscle injuries, together with the substantial burden associated with less frequent intra-articular knee injuries, highlights key priorities for injury prevention in professional football. Long-term surveillance within the same club provides valuable insights into evolving injury patterns and supports the development of targeted strategies to maximise player availability.

records.title: Lower Body Functional Test Performance Varies Based on Patient Demographics.
records.abstract: The utility of precise and instrumented musculoskeletal performance tests is essential to characterize musculoskeletal function during physical activity. Variation in these tests based on common patient demographics warrants consideration when using test results to counsel and advise physically active people. This study aimed to compare isolated muscle strength and functional performance outcomes by sex (male, female), age (late-stage adolescents: 18-21 years; adults: 22-34 years), and activity level (Tegner Activity Scale {TAS}: TAS ≥7, TAS <7). We hypothesized that males, adults, and individuals with higher activity levels would outperform their dichotomous pair. This is a cross-sectional study. A total of 185 healthy participants (sex: 112 female, 73 male; age: 21±3 years; height: 173±10 cm; mass: 71±12 kg) with no history of lower extremity surgery and no history of lower extremity injury within the previous six months participated in this study. Participants completed isokinetic knee extension/flexion at 90°/s and 180°/s, isometric knee extension/flexion at 90° of knee flexion, the single-leg hop for distance, the triple hop for distance, and the 6-m timed hop. Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels were stronger than females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels across all isolated muscle strength tests (p<0.05). Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels jumped farther and faster than females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels for all hop tests except the triple hop for distance. Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels consistently outperformed females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels, highlighting differences in performance by sex, age, and activity level. These findings suggest that personalization should be considered when using musculoskeletal performance tests to make important healthcare decisions during recovery from injury and/or surgery.

records.title: Management, reconstructive strategies and outcomes following open tibia/fibula and ankle fractures: An age-based comparison.
records.abstract: Open lower limb fractures require multidisciplinary orthoplastic management. With an ageing population, older patients present with distinct injury patterns, greater comorbidity and reduced physiological reserve. In this study, we compared presentation, management and outcomes between younger and older patients. A 4-year retrospective complete case cohort study (2018-2022) was conducted at a tertiary major trauma centre. Adult patients with open tibia, fibula or ankle fractures were included. Patients were stratified into younger adult (<65 years) and older adult (≥65 years) cohorts based on age. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, injury mechanism, Gustilo-Anderson (GA) classification, soft tissue reconstruction strategy, complications and mortality. A total of 292 patients were included (183 younger and 109 older adults). The older cohort were predominantly female (71%) with greater comorbidity burden. Despite the predominantly low-energy mechanisms (61% ground level falls), they sustained more severe injuries, with a higher proportion of GA grade III fractures, particularly GA-IIIb (52%). Single-stage skeletal fixation and soft tissue coverage was more frequently performed in older patients (55%). Median length of stay was longer (16 vs 10 days), and complications were comparable (20 vs 14%). In-hospital mortality was observed exclusively in the older cohort and occurred in 10% of the population-nearly half of which resulted from acute preoperative physiological decompensation. Older patients experience higher morbidity alongside greater comorbidity and severity of injury, despite lower energy mechanism. Management of injury frequently favours single-stage soft tissue coverage. This highlights the need for patient centred orthoplastic pathways and importance of early multidisciplinary involvement.

records.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
records.abstract: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases. A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05). Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047). Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management. (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes. III.

records.title: Metatarsal Strains During Loading and Motion of the Foot and Ankle in a Cadaveric Model.
records.abstract: Metatarsal bone stress injuries (BSI) are painful, overuse injuries commonly seen in athletes and military personnel. High strain magnitudes combined with repetitive loading cycles causes bone fatigue and microdamage accumulation. To protect against BSI, it is necessary to determine how to limit bone strain magnitude without sacrificing physical activity. This study examined maximum and minimum principal dorsal strains of metatarsals 2-4 during tibial dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, external/internal rotation, and varus/valgus alignment with four underfoot conditions. Five lower-limb cadaveric specimens were instrumented with strain gauges on metatarsals 2-4 and a robotic actuator applied 25% bodyweight and moved the ankle/foot through its envelope of passive motion. Dorsiflexion and varus tibial motion produced the greatest increase in strain magnitudes during all underfoot conditions. Adding half-inch blocks beneath the medial and lateral forefoot caused principal strain magnitudes to increase threefold within the metatarsals adjacent to the block across all motions. Passive engagement of the windlass mechanism during dorsiflexion caused approximately a threefold increase in maximum principal strain of metatarsals 2-3 coinciding with a significant decrease in metatarsal 4. The results emphasize the role that the arch and its supporting structures play in modulating metatarsal loading even within a passive model.

records.title: Minimally Invasive Revision Surgery Combining Endoscopic Double-Row Reinsertion and Flexor Hallucis Longus Transfer for Insertional Achilles Tendon Re-Rupture in a Semi-Professional Rugby Player: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute insertional Achilles tendon rupture (A-IATR) is a rare, often season-ending injury in athletes. Revision after a failed repair is particularly challenging, and return to sport (RTS) after such surgery is rarely documented. We report one such case. Methods: A 32-year-old semi-professional rugby prop forward sustained an insertional re-rupture eighteen months after open transosseous reinsertion without suture anchors. MRI showed complete detachment with 15 mm of retraction and no residual tendon on the footprint. A single-stage procedure combining endoscopic double-row (SpeedBridge™) reinsertion and flexor hallucis longus (FHL) transfer was performed, followed by six weeks of non-weight-bearing cast immobilization and criteria-based rehabilitation, with Ankle-GO™-guided return to play. Results: At three months, MRI showed tendon continuity without re-rupture. Return to play was authorized at 8.2 months (Ankle-GO™ 16/25); the patient returned to official competition at 9.4 months and was still competing approximately 17 months after surgery. At 15 months, the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score was 84 and the AOFAS score 90. No complication occurred. Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first report of RTS after this combined endoscopic revision technique. This single case suggests that this approach may be a feasible revision option in high-demand athletes; comparative studies are needed.

records.title: Navicular fractures in elite athletes: Clarifying the evidence base of the 2025 International Foot and Ankle Sports Consensus.
records.abstract: The recent international foot and ankle sports consensus and systematic review on navicular fractures in elite athletes addresses a highly relevant and challenging topic in sports medicine and provides valuable guidance in an area where standardized treatment and return to sport (RTS) recommendations remain limited. However, several methodological and reporting issues within the systematic review warrant clarification, given their potential influence on RTS decision-making. The reported mean RTS time of 8.2 weeks after operative treatment of navicular stress fractures appears to result from an error in the extraction of time units. Recalculation based on the included studies, after converting all values to weeks, yields a mean RTS of approximately 19.7 weeks (4.5 months), consistent with the expert consensus recommendation of 4-6 months after surgery. Further discrepancies concern the application of the stated eligibility criteria: 5 of the 14 included studies were published outside the specified 15-year window, and at least four involved cohorts with a mean age below 18 years despite paediatric studies being listed as an exclusion criterion. Further inconsistencies in study classification and reporting add to these concerns. We believe that clarification of these concerns is essential to ensure the reliability of the evidence base informing the consensus recommendations and to support accurate guidance for RTS decision-making in elite athletes with navicular fractures. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

records.title: Nonoperative Management of an Acute Complete Achilles Tendon Rupture With Mesenchymal Stem Cells and Extracellular Vesicles: A Case Report.
records.abstract: An acute complete rupture of the Achilles tendon with a large intertendinous gap is conventionally regarded as a surgical indication, yet operative repair carries a significant burden on wound-healing and potential for neurovascular complications, whereas nonoperative care may be limited by re-rupture and incomplete functional recovery. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (hUC-MSCs) and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) exert immunomodulatory, pro-angiogenic and pro-tenogenic paracrine effects that could support tendon healing. A healthy 45-year-old recreationally active male sustained an acute complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon while playing tennis. A 3.0-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a full-thickness mid-substance rupture located 6.1 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, with a 3.7 cm gap. He delayed treatment and opted out of surgical management and was offered nonoperative care with a combined biologic regimen: two ultrasound-guided intralesional injections of hUC-MSC-derived EVs (a total of 30 × 10⁹ vesicles) deposited into the tendon gap, both stumps, and the peritendon along with three consecutive daily intravenous (IV) infusions of hUC-MSCs (approximately 1.7 × 10⁶ cells/kg of total body weight) as a paracrine priming adjuvant, alongside an injury-guided functional rehabilitation program.  Pain measured using the numeric rating scale (NRS) decreased from 10/10 at baseline to 0/10 at six months post-intervention. At final follow-up (approx 14 months) the patient had returned to regular weight training and jogging without pain or functional limitations. On physical examination, the Thompson Test was negative, the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score (ATRS) and the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot scores were both calculated as 100/100, and instrumented biomechanical testing showed near-symmetric lower-limb range of motion and balance. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a remodeled tendon with restoration of continuity and no residual gap. No mild or severe adverse events were reported during or after procedures. In this single case report, a combined regimen of systemic hUC-MSCs and intralesional hUC-MSC-derived EVs was associated with imaging-confirmed tendon healing and full functional recovery of an acute complete Achilles tendon rupture managed nonoperatively. This treatment protocol serves as a hypothesis-generating observation with potential for validation in controlled prospective studies.

records.title: Novel understanding in diagnosis and management of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
records.abstract: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) is a common cause of exercise-related respiratory symptoms in athletes and is traditionally diagnosed by demonstrating airway narrowing following exercise or surrogate bronchoprovocation testing. Whilst this provides objective evidence of bronchoconstriction, it offers limited insight into the underlying pathophysiology of airway dysfunction. This review discusses emerging developments in EIB, focusing on biomarkers of airway inflammation and injury, respiratory oscillometry, breathing pattern assessment and wearable respiratory monitoring. The concept that EIB may represent the clinical manifestation of a broader process of airway injury and remodeling is also considered. Relevant literature was identified through searches of PubMed and Google Scholar with no lower date restriction to May 2026, supplemented by reference-list searching. The future challenge in EIB is no longer simply confirming bronchoconstriction but identifying athletes at risk of airway dysfunction before clinically significant disease develops. Emerging biomarkers, oscillometry and continuous respiratory monitoring may enable earlier phenotyping and more personalized management than conventional bronchoprovocation testing alone. Collectively, these approaches have the potential to shift EIB care from diagnosing established disease toward preserving airway health within a holistic model of athlete respiratory care.

records.title: Open Fractures in Polytrauma and Non-Polytrauma Patients: Outcomes and Predictive Factors in a Level III Trauma Center.
records.abstract: Open fractures represent complex injuries characterized by bone exposure, soft-tissue damage, and a high risk of infection, often requiring multidisciplinary management. In polytraumatized patients, these injuries further increase clinical complexity and hospital resource utilization. The purpose of this study was to evaluate adherence to international guidelines in the management of open fractures at a third-level trauma center and to identify clinical and organizational predictors of outcomes, complications, and hospitalization burden in polytraumatized and non-polytraumatized patients. A retrospective, single-center study was conducted including all patients treated for open fractures between January 2020 and December 2023. Demographic data, injury mechanisms, fracture location, Gustilo-Anderson grade, surgical timing, treatment strategy (Early Total Care or Damage Control Orthopedics), ICU admission, complications, and readmissions were collected. Polytrauma status was recorded. Primary outcomes included infection rate, length of hospital stay, number of admissions, and cumulative hospitalization time. Statistical analysis was performed using Student's t-test, Fisher's exact test, and Pearson correlation, with significance set at p < 0.05. A total of 115 patients were included, of whom 53 (46.1%) were polytraumatized. The mean age was 47.1 years, with a male predominance. Lower-limb fractures were most common, particularly involving the tibia. Grade III injuries accounted for 61.7% of cases. Surgical debridement was performed within 6 hours in 65.2% of patients. External fixation for damage control was used in 73% of cases, with a mean fixation duration of 103 days. Postoperative ICU admission was required in 27.8% of patients. Overall infection rate was 15.7%. Polytraumatized patients experienced significantly longer hospital stays and a higher number of readmissions, but polytrauma status was not associated with increased infection risk. Higher Gustilo-Anderson grade showed a strong correlation with prolonged hospitalization and infection. Damage control strategies were associated with longer cumulative hospitalization and more frequent readmissions but not with higher infection rates. These findings indicate that fracture severity and local tissue damage, rather than polytrauma status itself, are the main determinants of infection risk and hospitalization burden. While polytrauma increases overall resource utilization, standardized multidisciplinary management allows comparable orthopedic outcomes. Damage control orthopedics remains essential in severe cases but implies longer and more fragmented care pathways. In a high-volume trauma center adhering to international guidelines, open fracture outcomes are primarily driven by injury severity. Polytrauma influences hospitalization burden but not infection risk. Awareness of these factors is essential for optimizing trauma pathways, resource allocation, and patient counseling.

records.title: Oral contraceptive use and anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction in women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of very low-certainty evidence.
records.abstract: To determine whether oral contraceptive use is associated with anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction in women and to examine whether associations vary according to age, contraceptive formulation, duration of use and outcome definition. PubMed, Scopus, Embase and Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS) were searched through 31 July 2026 (LILACS rerun with multilingual terms on 16 September 2026). Comparative observational studies were meta-analysed. The primary analysis pooled adjusted or matched odds ratios (ORs) for reconstruction or operatively treated injury using random-effects restricted maximum-likelihood models with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed with risk of bias in nonrandomised studies of exposures and certainty with grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation. Ten studies were included; seven were meta-analysed. The primary analysis (four studies) showed no clear association (OR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.77-1.02; I 2 = 84%; τ 2 = 0.01; 95% prediction interval, 0.66-1.19). Two crude athlete studies and the active-comparator cohort (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.89-1.01) also had CIs including 1. Adding one crude database estimate yielded OR 0.85 (95% CI, 0.74-0.98; I 2 = 90%; 95% prediction interval, 0.61-1.19). Leave-one-out results were unstable. The certainty of evidence was very low. The primary adjusted or matched analysis did not establish a clear association between oral contraceptive use and anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or operatively treated injury; substantial heterogeneity, residual confounding and very low certainty of evidence preclude causal interpretation. Current evidence does not support initiating or selecting oral contraceptives for anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention. Well-designed prospective studies with standardised exposure and outcome definitions are needed. Level IV, systematic review of observational studies.
